units.title: Autoencoders and latent-variable models
outcomes: Derive a mixture-of-Gaussians marginal and state the prior, likelihood and marginal of the nonlinear latent variable model.
Explain why the VAE is a training architecture while the learned model is the nonlinear latent variable model.
Contrast a plain autoencoder bottleneck with a probabilistic latent model that defines \(\Pr(x)\).
units.why: Every later unit reuses the same split: a prior over \(z\), a decoder likelihood, and an approximate posterior. If this split is vague, the ELBO looks like bookkeeping instead of a bound.

next.note: Turn the prior and likelihood into the ELBO and a trainable sampler.
Keep the autoencoder versus probabilistic distinction for the family comparison.

study.title: Latent variable models and the nonlinear generator
study.locator: Sections 17.1 and 17.2, with Equations 17.1 to 17.7 (pp. 327 to 330)
study.depth: Stop before Section 17.3. Training and the ELBO belong to the next unit.

study.title: Notebook 17.1: latent variable models
study.locator: The notebook that accompanies Sections 17.1 and 17.2, margin-noted beside Equation 17.7

focus: The marginal \(\Pr(x) = \int \Pr(x \mid z) \Pr(z) \, dz\) sums over every latent cause. The mixture example (Eq 17.4) is the discrete case; the nonlinear model (Eq 17.7) replaces the table with a network \(f[z, \phi]\).

The prior is fixed to \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (Eq 17.5) while the likelihood \(\mathcal{N}(f[z, \phi], \sigma^2 I)\) carries the parameters (Eq 17.6). Generation samples \(z\) first and never touches the encoder.
The chapter introduction warns that calling the VAE the model of \(\Pr(x)\) misleads. The final model is a nonlinear latent variable model with no variational and no autoencoder parts.

A plain autoencoder minimizes reconstruction through a bottleneck and defines no distribution. The probabilistic model adds prior, likelihood and posterior, which is what makes a likelihood bound possible.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write Equations 17.1, 17.2 and 17.7 from memory, then state the prior, likelihood and generation path for a 2D latent and 1D observation.
traps: Reading the encoder as part of the generative model. Generation draws \(z\) from the prior and decodes; the encoder only proposes \(q\) during training.
Treating a low reconstruction error as a likelihood claim. Autoencoders have no \(\Pr(x)\), so their error cannot be compared with ELBO or flow likelihood numbers.

selfTest.q: A 1D mixture of Gaussians has 5 components. How many raw parameters does it need, and how many are free?
selfTest.a: 15 raw numbers: 5 means, 5 variances and 5 weights. Weights lie in [0,1] and sum to 1, which removes one degree of freedom, so 14 are free. Means are real and variances are positive.

selfTest.q: Why does the book say the VAE is an architecture, not the model of \(\Pr(x)\)?
selfTest.a: The learned model is the nonlinear latent variable model: prior \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) plus decoder likelihood. The encoder and the sampling step only help optimize the bound and are absent from the final \(\Pr(x)\).

selfTest.q: How does a plain autoencoder differ from the VAE bottleneck?
selfTest.a: An autoencoder learns a low-dimensional code that reconstructs well and defines no distribution. A VAE learns a prior, a likelihood and an approximate posterior, so it defines \(\Pr(x)\) and a lower bound on its \(\log\) likelihood.

selfTest.q: How do you generate from the Section 17.2 model?
selfTest.a: Draw \(z\) from \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\), compute \(f[z, \phi]\), then draw \(x\) from \(\mathcal{N}(f[z, \phi], \sigma^2 I)\). The encoder plays no role.

practice.name: UDL Problems 17.1 to 17.3: MoG parameters, log concavity and Jensen

units.title: The ELBO and reparameterized sampling
outcomes: Derive the ELBO from Jensen and split it into a reconstruction term and a KL term against the prior.
Implement the one-sample VAE loss with separate reconstruction and KL terms that match the public tests.
Implement reparameterized sampling so gradients flow through the encoder mean and variance.
units.why: The ELBO is the only training signal in the required VAE build. A sign error in the KL term or a blocked sampler fails silently into blurry reconstructions.

next.note: Watch the KL term collapse to zero during training.
The diffusion loss is another ELBO with the same reconstruction-versus-prior shape.

study.title: ELBO derivation and the reconstruction-minus-KL form
study.locator: Sections 17.3 to 17.6, with Equations 17.14 to 17.24 (pp. 331 to 338)
study.depth: Read Section 17.6.1 for the one-sample estimate (Eq 17.23). Leave Sections 17.8 to 17.9 and the Notes for later units.

study.title: The reparameterization trick
study.locator: Section 17.7 with Equation 17.25 and Notebook 17.2 (pp. 339 to 340)

focus: Jensen turns \(\log \mathbb{E}\) into \(\mathbb{E} \log\) and creates the bound (Eqs 17.14 to 17.16). Equation 17.17 shows the gap to the true log likelihood is exactly \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q \,\|\, \text{posterior}]\), so the bound is tight when \(q\) equals the posterior.

Equation 17.18 rewrites the same bound as expected log likelihood minus \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q \,\|\, \text{prior}]\). Section 17.6 conditions \(q\) on \(x\) to get the VAE form (Eq 17.21) with encoder networks for mean and covariance.
The one-sample estimate (Eq 17.23) pairs one decoded log likelihood with the closed-form Gaussian KL (Eq 17.24). Keep the two terms separate in code so collapse is visible.
Reparameterization (Eq 17.25) moves randomness into \(\epsilon\) from \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\). Backprop passes through \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) and never down the stochastic branch.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive Equation 17.18 from Equation 17.16 in four lines, then compute the Deep-ML 393 check (0.5 reconstruction, 2.5 KL, 3.0 total) with NumPy.
traps: Coding `std` as `exp(logvar)` instead of `exp(0.5 logvar)`. The samples then have variance \(\sigma^4\) while the KL in Eq 17.24 assumes \(\sigma^2\).
Averaging the KL over the wrong axis. The closed form sums over latent dimensions first and then averages over the batch; swapping the two changes the loss scale with latent size.

Comparing the Equation 17.30 objective with an ordinary ELBO. With \(\beta\) above 1 it is still a lower bound on \(\log \Pr(x)\), but a looser one, so its value is not comparable with the \(\beta = 1\) bound.

selfTest.q: State the ELBO in reconstruction-minus-KL form and say when it is tight.
selfTest.a: \(\mathrm{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_q[\log \Pr(x \mid z, \phi)] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q \,\|\, \text{prior}]\) (Eqs 17.18 and 17.21). It equals \(\log \Pr(x \mid \phi)\) minus \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q \,\|\, \text{posterior}]\) (Eq 17.17), so it is tight exactly when \(q\) equals the true posterior.

selfTest.q: Write the reparameterized sample and explain why gradients flow.
selfTest.a: \(z^* = \mu + \Sigma^{1/2} \epsilon\) with \(\epsilon\) from \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (Eq 17.25). Randomness enters through \(\epsilon\), which has no parameters, so gradients flow through \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) and skip the stochastic branch.

selfTest.q: For `x=[[1,0]]`, `x_hat=[[0.5,0.5]]`, `mu=[[1,2]]` and `log_var=[[0,0]]`, what does Deep-ML 393 return?
selfTest.a: (3.0, 0.5, 2.5). Reconstruction 0.5 is the summed squared error 0.25 + 0.25. KL 2.5 is 0.5 times (1 + 4). Total is their sum.

selfTest.q: Why does the VAE use one sample per data point in Equation 17.23?
selfTest.a: The expectation over \(q\) is estimated by Monte Carlo with \(N = 1\) while the KL stays closed-form. One sample per point is unbiased and keeps the per-step cost low; more samples only reduce estimator variance.

units.title: Posterior collapse and decoder capacity
outcomes: Detect posterior collapse from per-dimension KL and from resampling tests on a small VAE.
Explain why a high-capacity decoder lets the ELBO keep reconstruction while the KL goes to zero.
Apply KL annealing and decoder-capacity bounds and state what each intervention cannot prove.
units.why: Collapse is the characteristic VAE failure: the loss looks fine while the latent code carries nothing. The checkpoint requires you to produce it on purpose and then bound it.

next.note: A collapsed model is the case study for why loss and samples prove different things.
Compare latent-ignoring collapse with GAN mode collapse.

study.title: Posterior collapse and the information preference note
study.locator: Notes: the Posterior collapse paragraph and the Chen et al. paragraph (p. 346)

study.title: Disentanglement and the \(\beta\)-weighted loss
study.depth: Equation 17.30 with \(\beta\) above 1 is still a lower bound, only a looser one. The Notes sentence about gradually increasing the KL term describes annealing: the KL weight starts near 0 and rises to 1.

focus: Collapse means the encoder outputs the prior for every input: per-dimension KL sits near zero and resampling \(z\) leaves reconstructions and samples unchanged.
Chen et al. observed the mechanism: with a PixelCNN-class likelihood the decoder models \(x\) alone, so the ELBO keeps reconstruction while the KL term pays for nothing and is driven to zero.
\(\beta\) above 1 in Eq 17.30 pushes \(q\) harder toward the prior and raises collapse risk. Annealing starts the KL weight at 0 and raises it to 1 so the code is used before it is taxed.
The book names VQ-VAE style discrete latents and total-correlation penalties as further directions. Treat them as pointers, not as claims you verified here.
units.reproduce: Train a tiny VAE on a 2D mixture twice: once with KL weight 1 and once with a large weight such as \(\beta = 10\) (or a decoder that also sees \(x\)). Log per-dimension KL each epoch. In the collapsed run, show that KL sits near zero and that decoding fresh prior samples gives nearly the same output. Then add annealing from 0 to 1 to the weight-1 run and state the schedule you used.
traps: Reading a falling total loss as learning. In collapse the reconstruction term improves while the KL term dies; only the split plot shows it.
Raising the KL weight to fix blurry samples. A larger final weight pressures \(q\) toward the prior and makes collapse more likely, not less.

selfTest.q: What is posterior collapse in one observable sentence?
selfTest.a: The encoder predicts the prior for every input: per-dimension KL is near zero and resampling \(z\) does not change reconstructions or samples.

selfTest.q: Why does a powerful autoregressive decoder invite collapse?
selfTest.a: It can model \(x\) without \(z\), so the ELBO keeps the reconstruction term while the KL term is pure cost. Optimization then sets \(q\) to the prior.

selfTest.q: What does \(\beta\) above 1 in Equation 17.30 do to collapse risk?
selfTest.a: It raises the KL penalty, which pushes \(q\) toward the prior and makes collapse more likely. The objective stays a lower bound, only a looser one.

selfTest.q: Name two measurements that expose collapse.
selfTest.a: Per-dimension KL near zero across epochs, and a resampling test where fresh \(z\) with a fixed decoder leaves outputs unchanged while the loss barely moves.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a controlled collapse run with per-dimension KL logs, a decoder-capacity ablation, KL annealing from 0 to 1, and a resampling test.
units.stopWhen: Your split KL plot shows collapse on demand, annealing restores nonzero KL, and the resampling test passes with the schedule written down.

fit.note: The Notes collapse paragraph plus Eq 17.30 support measure depth, with collapse practice assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: GAN objectives, alternating updates and mode collapse
outcomes: Derive the minimax losses, the optimal discriminator, and the Jensen-Shannon form of the generator signal.
Run alternating D-then-G updates with the non-saturating generator loss on a small GAN.
Distinguish mode dropping from mode collapse and name the imbalance that causes each.
units.why: GANs are the adversarial counterpoint to likelihood training: no density, a learned loss, and failures that look like good samples. The minimax argument explains why.

next.note: Good samples with dropped modes motivate precision-recall evaluation.
Compare GAN mode collapse with VAE posterior collapse.

study.title: Minimax, optimal discriminator and the Jensen-Shannon split
study.locator: Sections 15.1 to 15.2.2 with Equations 15.2 to 15.9 (pp. 276 to 283)

study.title: Wasserstein, DCGAN recipe and collapse
study.locator: Sections 15.2.3 to 15.2.6 on Wasserstein (pp. 284 to 286); Section 15.1.3 DCGAN recipe and Section 15.1.4 with Figure 15.5 on mode dropping and collapse (pp. 279 to 281)
study.depth: Skip Sections 15.3 to 15.6 here: progressive growing, conditional GANs, translation and StyleGAN are later material.

study.title: Basic GAN on a 2D Gaussian
study.locator: Generate Some Real Data, Generator, Discriminator and Training: 2D Gaussian with `A=[[1,2],[-0.1,0.5]]` and `b=[1,2]`, linear generator, 3-layer Tanh discriminator, batch size 8, \(D\) updated before \(G\) each iteration

study.title: DCGAN blocks and Pokemon training
study.locator: The Generator with `G_block` and the 100-dim latent to 64 by 64 map; Discriminator with `D_block` and leaky ReLU 0.2; Training with Adam `beta1` 0.5

focus: Equations 15.2 to 15.5 turn binary cross-entropy into a minimax game. The practical generator loss is the non-saturating \(-\log D(G(z))\) (label flipped to 1), because the \(\max \log(1 - D)\) form saturates when \(D\) is confident.

Section 15.2.1 shows the optimal discriminator is \(\Pr(x)/[\Pr(x) + \Pr(\text{fake})]\), and the loss becomes a Jensen-Shannon divergence split into quality and coverage terms. The book notes that the real-data term of Eq 15.6 does not involve the generator, so nothing directly rewards it for covering missed modes; it calls this the putative reason for mode dropping.

Section 15.1.4 separates the failures: mode dropping generates a realistic subset (no beards), while collapse maps most \(z\) to one or few points and ignores \(z\). Figure 15.5 and the Notes diversity paragraph make this concrete.

The DCGAN recipe is strided convolutions, `BatchNorm` in both nets, leaky ReLU in \(D\) and Adam with `beta1` 0.5. D2L updates \(D\) first each iteration with detached fakes so no gradient reaches \(G\) through the \(D\) step.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two losses of Equation 15.5 and the non-saturating generator loss. Then run the D2L basic GAN for 20 epochs at `lr_D` 0.05 and `lr_G` 0.005 and watch the discriminator loss move toward about 0.69 (\(\log 2\), the value when \(D\) outputs 0.5 everywhere) as the fake scatter covers the real Gaussian.
traps: Forgetting `detach` on `fake_X` in the \(D\) step. The \(D\) loss then backpropagates into \(G\): wasted compute, and if \(G\)'s gradients are not zeroed before its own step, \(G\) also moves in the direction that helps \(D\).

Following the DCGAN summary line about `BatchNorm` literally. The shipped `D_block` applies `BatchNorm` in every block including the first, while the paper recipe uses no norm on the discriminator input. Implement the paper variant and note the difference.

Reading \(D\) accuracy 0.5 as proof of distributional match. A finite-capacity \(D\) reaches chance on a mode-dropped generator too; the Notes duplicate test shows support can be far smaller than the training set.

selfTest.q: Write the two alternating losses and the update order.
selfTest.a: \(D\) minimizes BCE on real data with label 1 and detached fakes with label 0. \(G\) minimizes \(-\log D(G(z))\), the same BCE with fake labels flipped to 1. Each iteration updates \(D\) first, then \(G\).

selfTest.q: Why can the generator ignore coverage, according to Section 15.2.1?
selfTest.a: In Equation 15.6 the real-data term does not involve \(G\), so for a fixed discriminator the generator's gradient comes only from its own samples. Generating a realistic subset is not penalized directly. The book offers this as the putative reason for mode dropping.

selfTest.q: Distinguish mode dropping from mode collapse.
selfTest.a: Dropping covers a realistic subset of modes. Collapse maps most or all \(z\) to one or few points and ignores the latent input.

selfTest.q: For uniform \([0, 1]\) versus \([a, a+1]\) with \(a = 2\), give KL, JS and W1.
selfTest.a: Both KL directions are infinite because the supports are disjoint. JS is \(\log 2\) (1 bit). W1 is \(|a| = 2\).

practice.locator: Training with `update_D` and `update_G`: batch size 8, latent dim 2, 20 epochs; confirm \(D\) runs before \(G\) and fakes use `detach`
practice.note: Plot real versus fake scatter at epochs 1, 5 and 20, and add a discriminator-accuracy printout. State the epoch where accuracy first nears 0.5, and remember that chance accuracy does not prove the distributions match.

practice.name: UDL Problem 15.4: divergences for shifted uniforms
practice.locator: Problem 15.4 (p. 303): KL, reverse KL, JS and Wasserstein for uniform \([0, 1]\) versus \([a, a+1]\) over \(a\) in \([-3, 3]\)

units.title: Diffusion: forward corruption, reverse denoising and prediction targets
outcomes: Derive the one-step forward kernel, the closed-form \(x_0\)-to-\(x_t\) sampler and the reverse conditional used for training.
Derive the diffusion ELBO down to the per-step noise matching loss of Algorithm 18.1.
Recognize noise, data and velocity prediction targets and state when each stays stable.
units.why: Diffusion training is ELBO arithmetic plus one Gaussian closure. Once the closed form and the noise-to-data map are routine, schedules and samplers become cost choices.

next.note: Turn the trained denoiser into a sampler with a schedule and guidance.

study.title: Forward encoder and closed-form sampling
study.locator: Sections 18.1 and 18.2 with Equations 18.1 to 18.8 and Figures 18.2 and 18.3 (pp. 349 to 353)

study.title: Reverse decoder, ELBO and the noise reparameterization
study.locator: Sections 18.3 to 18.5 with Equations 18.16 to 18.40 and Algorithm 18.1 (pp. 356 to 363)

study.title: Velocity parameterization
study.locator: Section 4: the \(v = \alpha \epsilon - \sigma x\) definition with \(\hat{x} = \alpha z_t - \sigma \hat{v}\), and the low signal-to-noise stability argument
study.depth: Read only the parameterization and loss-weighting discussion. Leave Algorithms 1 and 2 and all distillation results for later.

focus: The forward kernel is \(q(z_t \mid z_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{1 - \beta_t} z_{t-1}, \beta_t I)\) (Eq 18.2). Products of Gaussians close in closed form: \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \epsilon\) with \(\bar{\alpha}_t\) the product of \((1 - \beta_s)\) (Eqs 18.7 and 18.8).

The reverse conditional \(q(z_{t-1} \mid z_t, x)\) (Eq 18.15) trains the decoder. The ELBO (Eq 18.25) becomes per-step KL terms that reduce to squared error between the true reverse mean and \(f_t\) (Eqs 18.28 and 18.29).

Section 18.5 converts data prediction into noise prediction through Eq 18.30 and trains \(g\) to output \(\epsilon\) with the plain loss of Eq 18.40. The map is linear, so the two targets carry the same information with different conditioning.

Velocity \(v = \alpha \epsilon - \sigma x\) keeps the implied \(x\) prediction stable when signal-to-noise goes to zero, where \(\epsilon\)-to-\(x\) division by \(\alpha\) blows up. UDL never names it, so the paper supplies this one recognition item.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the three-step closed form of Problem 18.3 from Equations 18.5 to 18.7, then verify with NumPy that \(x_0=[1,2]\) at \(t=3\) with \(\epsilon=[0.5,-0.5]\) on `linspace(0.1,0.2,5)` gives `[1.1057,1.3488]`.
traps: Scaling the mean by \(1 - \beta\) instead of \(\sqrt{1 - \beta}\). The square root is what keeps the variance at 1 when the input has unit variance (Problem 18.1); without it the signal shrinks faster than the noise is added.
Indexing \(\bar{\alpha}\) at \(t\) instead of \(t - 1\) in the reverse mean. The coefficient \((1 - \alpha_{t-1})/(1 - \alpha_t)\) in Eq 18.28 is sensitive to this shift; test \(t = 1\) separately.
Treating noise, data and velocity targets as different models. They parameterize the same reverse mean; only their numerical behavior at low signal-to-noise differs.

selfTest.q: Write the one-step forward kernel and the direct \(x_0\)-to-\(x_t\) sampler.
selfTest.a: \(q(z_t \mid z_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{1 - \beta_t} z_{t-1}, \beta_t I)\). Then \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \epsilon\) with \(\bar{\alpha}_t\) the product of \((1 - \beta_s)\) over \(s = 1\) to \(t\).

selfTest.q: With a linear \(\beta\) schedule `linspace(0.1,0.2,5)`, what is \(x_1\) for `x0=[1.0]` and `eps=[1.0]`?
How are noise prediction and data prediction related?
selfTest.a: By \(x = (z_t - \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t} \epsilon)/\sqrt{\alpha_t}\) (Eqs 18.30 and 18.31). UDL trains \(g\) to predict \(\epsilon\) (Eqs 18.35 to 18.40); the data estimate follows by this linear map.

selfTest.q: State the velocity target and why it helps.
selfTest.a: \(v = \alpha_t \epsilon - \sigma_t x\) with \(\hat{x} = \alpha_t z_t - \sigma_t \hat{v}\). It stays well scaled at zero signal-to-noise, where converting an \(\epsilon\) prediction to \(x\) divides by \(\alpha\) near zero.

practice.name: UDL Problems 18.1 to 18.3: variance preservation and the closed form
practice.locator: Problems 18.1 to 18.3 (pp. 372 to 373): covariance preservation, combining two noises, and the three-step expansion to Eq 18.45

units.title: Diffusion sampling schedules, cost and guidance
outcomes: Explain why ancestral sampling needs about 1000 serial U-Net evals and what DDIM changes.
Compare step-count versus quality trade-offs including the 50-step DDIM point and cascades.
Distinguish classifier guidance from classifier-free guidance and predict the stereotyping effect of overweighting.
units.why: A trained denoiser is not yet a generator. Sampling cost and conditioning decide whether the model is usable, and both are set after training.

next.note: Judge sampling shortcuts by coverage and cost, not by cherry-picked images.

study.title: Implementation: U-Net, time embedding, DDIM and cascades
study.locator: Section 18.6 with Algorithms 18.1 and 18.2 and Notebooks 18.3 and 18.4 (pp. 363 to 368)

study.title: Conditioning and guidance
study.locator: Sections 18.6.3 and 18.6.4 with Equation 18.41 on classifier guidance and the classifier-free paragraph (pp. 365 to 368)
study.depth: Read for schedule, step-count and guidance mechanics at recognition depth. Do not train a large image model here.

focus: One U-Net maps \(z_t\) to an \(\epsilon\) estimate at one noise level, conditioned on a sinusoidal time embedding. Ancestral sampling (Algorithm 18.2) calls it serially about 1000 times per image, so cost scales with steps, not with parameters alone.

DDIM is a deterministic integrator of the probability-flow ODE: it drops per-step noise and gives good samples in about 50 steps on the book example. The Notes add latent-space diffusion as the further speedup used by Stable Diffusion.

Classifier guidance adds \(\sigma_t^2\) times \(\operatorname{grad} \log \Pr(c \mid z_t)\) from a separate noisy classifier (Eq 18.41). Classifier-free guidance trains \(g(z_t, \phi_t, c)\) with randomly dropped labels and mixes conditional and unconditional scores at sample time.
Overweighting the conditioning improves apparent quality but produces stereotyped outputs. The book draws the same trade as GAN truncation: less variety for cleaner exemplars.
units.reproduce: Write Algorithm 18.2 (ancestral sampling) from memory, then write how a deterministic DDIM sampler on a 50-step subsequence changes it. Count network evaluations per sample for both, 1000 against 50, and if you trained a model in the CS231n notebook, time both samplers.
traps: Calling DDIM faster per step. The gain is fewer steps with a different integrator, not a cheaper network; one DDIM step costs about the same as one ancestral step.
Reading guidance scale as likelihood tempering. It reweights the conditional score at sample time and changes coverage; it does not retrain the density.
Comparing step counts across different noise schedules. Fifty steps under one schedule is not the same compute-quality point as fifty under another; always fix the schedule first.

selfTest.q: Why is diffusion sampling slow, in one line of arithmetic?
selfTest.a: Each reverse step needs one full U-Net eval and good ancestral images need about 1000 serial steps, so one sample costs about 1000 network passes.

selfTest.q: What does DDIM change?
selfTest.a: It integrates the probability-flow ODE deterministically without per-step noise, so the book gets good samples in about 50 steps. It is still slower than most GAN sampling.

selfTest.q: Contrast classifier guidance with classifier-free guidance.
selfTest.a: Classifier guidance adds the gradient of a separately trained noisy classifier (Eq 18.41). Classifier-free guidance folds the class into the denoiser, drops it at random during training, and mixes conditional and unconditional predictions at sample time.

selfTest.q: What happens when conditioning is over-weighted?
selfTest.a: Higher apparent quality but stereotyped, low-variety samples. UDL notes the same quality-variety trade as GAN truncation.

units.title: Evaluating and comparing generative model families
outcomes: State what likelihood, ELBO, reconstructions and samples each prove and what each hides.
Compute Inception Score limits, FID behavior and precision-recall splits for a stated failure.
Contrast flows, VAEs, GANs and diffusion by likelihood, sampling, coverage, stability and evaluation at recognition depth.

study.title: What makes a good model and how to quantify it

study.title: Flow likelihood contrast at recognition depth
study.locator: Sections 16.1 to 16.2 with Equations 16.1 to 16.3, and Section 16.3.3 coupling Equations 16.13 and 16.14 (pp. 304 to 312)
study.depth: Read flows only far enough to state the change-of-variables likelihood and why coupling keeps the Jacobian triangular. Leave residual, autoregressive and multiscale flow details for later.

focus: Test likelihood needs a density: flows give it exactly (Eqs 16.1 to 16.3), VAE and diffusion give a lower bound, and GANs give nothing because they only sample. Training likelihood is not a generalization claim.

Inception Score (Eqs 14.2 and 14.3) rewards one realistic example per ImageNet class under one classifier. FID fits Gaussians to Inception features of real and fake sets, so it sees within-class spread but only through retained features. Precision-recall splits the two: realism versus coverage via \(k\)-nearest hyperspheres.
Figure 14.3 summarizes the trade: no family has efficient sampling, top quality, full coverage, a good latent space and exact likelihood at once. Quote the row, not a slogan.

Coupling (Eqs 16.13 and 16.14) leaves half the variables fixed and applies an invertible elementwise map to the rest with params from the fixed half. The Jacobian is triangular, so the determinant is the diagonal product and both directions stay cheap.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the Problem 16.1 density \(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x}}\) and check its integral equals 1, then fill one Figure 14.3 row per family from memory.
traps: Comparing likelihood numbers across families or preprocessings. VAE and diffusion report bounds, flows report exact values, and any dequantization or resolution change breaks comparability.

Reporting one FID from few samples or mismatched Inception weights. FID is a distribution distance under a Gaussian fit; small sample counts and different feature layers move it without any model change.
Treating low FID as proof of coverage. A mode-dropped GAN can score well; only the recall side or a duplicate test like the Notes 400-sample argument addresses support size.

selfTest.q: Which families give exact likelihood, a lower bound, or nothing?
selfTest.a: Flows give exact likelihood by change of variables. VAE and diffusion give a lower bound through the ELBO. GANs give no density; they sample without evaluating probabilities.

selfTest.q: State the 1D flow density for uniform \(z\) through \(x = z^2\).
selfTest.a: \(\Pr(x) = \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x}}\) on \((0, 1]\). The CDF is \(P(X \le x) = \sqrt{x}\); differentiate to get the density, which integrates to 1.

selfTest.q: Why is Inception Score insufficient, and what do FID and precision-recall add?
selfTest.a: IS needs ImageNet classes and one classifier and rewards a single good example per class. FID compares Gaussian-fitted Inception features of both sets, capturing within-class spread through retained features. Precision-recall splits realism (fakes inside the real manifold) from coverage (real data inside the fake manifold).

selfTest.q: How does coupling keep flows tractable?
selfTest.a: Half the variables pass through unchanged while the rest get an elementwise invertible map with parameters from the fixed half. The Jacobian is triangular, so its determinant is the product of diagonal terms and both directions stay cheap.
